abstract:
Term coding provides a common algebraic framework for network coding,
index coding and problems in extremal combinatorics. We exhibit a
decision problem in which lowering an output threshold by just one
changes the complexity from polynomial time to undecidability: no
algorithm then halts with the correct answer on every input.
The problem concerns dispersion, the maximum number of distinct output
tuples obtainable by interpreting the function symbols in a tuple of
terms on a finite alphabet. We restrict inputs by inequalities between
terms and ask whether a given instance meets a prescribed output
threshold for some alphabet size at least two. Both thresholds are
considered on the same class of instances.
A machine-checked Lean development and an interactive presentation of
the paper accompany this work
(GitHub: \PaperThreeLeanGitHub; DOI: \PaperThreeLeanDOI);
Section~\ref{sec:open} specifies its external input and verification limits.

An expression such as $f(g(x),y)$ becomes a function of $x,y$ once a set

expressions \emph{terms}, and the choice of functions an
\emph{interpretation}. Every occurrence of a symbol uses the same
function: for example, $g(g(x))$ means that this function is applied
twice. A tuple of terms in variables $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ defines a map
from $A^m$ to $A^r$, where $r$ is the number of terms in the tuple.
We restrict its domain by requiring finitely many inequalities
$u\ne v$ between terms. Such inequalities are also called
\emph{disequalities} or \emph{tests}.

The algorithm uses a graph determined by the terms. Its vertices are
the distinct subterms, together with all declared variables; an edge
runs from an immediate argument to the term containing it. This is a
directed acyclic graph. A \emph{term cut} is a set of vertices meeting
every directed path from a variable to an output term. Paths of length
zero are included, and a cut may contain variables or output terms.
Let $\rho_\Gamma$ be the minimum size of such a cut. Every cut for an
instance in $\mathcal C$ contains $x,y$, since each is both a variable
and an output. Thus $\rho_\Gamma\ge2$.

\label{thm:main}
For every fixed integer $k\ge2$, the following decision problems on
$\mathcal C$ have the indicated complexities:
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
 \text{input: }\Gamma\in\mathcal C&
 \exists n\ge2:\ D_\Gamma(n)\ge b_k(n)&\text{undecidable},\\[2pt]
 \text{input: }\Gamma\in\mathcal C&
 \exists n\ge2:\ D_\Gamma(n)\ge b_k(n)+1&\text{polynomial time}.
\end{array}
\]
The second answer is yes if and only if no test has syntactically
identical sides and $\rho_\Gamma\ge k+1$. This criterion can also be
decided in polynomial time when $k\ge2$ is part of the input, written
in binary. If it holds, and $s$ is the number of distinct subterms in
the outputs and tests together with all declared variables, then
\[
 D_\Gamma(n)\ge\lfloor n/s\rfloor^{k+1}\quad(n\ge s).
\]
In particular, whenever the criterion holds, the strict threshold is
attained at the alphabet size $n_0=s^{k+1}$.
For every fixed $k$, the first problem remains undecidable on the
subclass with $\rho_\Gamma=k$, where $D_\Gamma(n)\le b_k(n)$ for all
$n\ge2$. There is no total computable function $B$ such that every
positive instance in this subclass, of input length $N$, has a size
$n$ with $2\le n\le B(N)$ and $D_\Gamma(n)=b_k(n)$.

For outputs $(x,y)$, the test $x\ne y$ allows at most $n(n-1)$ outputs.
Achieving this number means that every pair $(a,b)$ with $a\ne b$
satisfies every test. In particular, if a further test is $F(x)\ne y$,
then $F(a)=a$ for every $a$: otherwise the pair $(a,F(a))$ would fail.
We refer to equality with this upper bound as \emph{saturation}.
Applying this observation to terms expressing inverse and relator laws
forces them to hold on the whole finite set. Section~\ref{sec:reduction}
uses it to encode the following undecidable problem for one fixed
finitely presented group: given a word, does it have nonidentity image
in some finite quotient? The external group-theoretic result is
\cite[Theorem 2.1]{BW}. Only the term representing the input word varies;
the unary symbols and the number of tests are fixed.
Adding $k-2$ new variables as further outputs, with no tests involving
them, multiplies the image size by $n^{k-2}$ and proves the other degrees.

Riis and Gadouleau \cite{RG} proved that ordinary dispersion, without
tests, has growth exponent equal to the minimum term cut. Their lower
bound transmits independent values along disjoint paths in the term
graph. Each transmitted value is accompanied by a label identifying
its subterm, so that different uses of a symbol can be handled by one
function. This construction is called \emph{routing}.
Section~\ref{sec:routing} shows that the same labels satisfy every test
whose sides are syntactically different. It also proves the sharper
upper bound
\[
 D_\Gamma(n)\le n^{\rho_\Gamma}-n^{\rho_\Gamma-1}
 \qquad(\Gamma\in\mathcal C),
\]
because every cut contains the output variables $x,y$, whose values
must differ. These two bounds give the strict decision criterion.
The reduction uses the new identity-forcing argument above; it does
not follow from the earlier asymptotic theorem.

For the two-variable instance associated to a fixed presentation $G$
and a word $w$, write $D_{G,w}(n)$ for the dispersion.
For every nonempty word $w$, Section~\ref{sec:near} constructs functions
satisfying
\[
 n(n-1)-Mn\le D_{G,w}(n)\le n(n-1)\qquad(n>|w|),
\]
where $|w|$ counts the letters as written and $M$ depends only on the
presentation. Given $w$ and a positive rational $\varepsilon$, the
construction computes an integer $n\ge2$ and unary functions for which
the allowed output image contains at least $(1-\varepsilon)n(n-1)$ pairs. It works even
for words for which equality with $n(n-1)$ is impossible at every size.
Thus arbitrarily accurate proportions of this upper bound, with
computable witnesses, do not decide whether the bound can be reached.
The reason is concrete: each failed identity at a point excludes at
most one further second coordinate. At most $Mn$ pairs are lost, a
vanishing proportion of $n(n-1)$, whereas losing no pair forces every
identity to hold everywhere. The approximate constructions need not
satisfy the group laws.

\label{ex:nonvacuity}
Fix $k\ge2$, variables $x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1}$, and only the test
$x_1\ne x_2$. The output tuple $(x_1,\ldots,x_{k+1})$ has
$b_{k+1}(n)$ distinct outputs and exceeds $b_k(n)+1$ already at $n=2$.
With the same variables, test and number of output coordinates, the
tuple $(x_1,\ldots,x_k,x_1)$ instead has exactly $b_k(n)$ outputs.
It gives a no answer to the strict question and a yes answer to the
non-strict question. Adding the deliberately impossible test $x_1\ne x_1$
excludes every assignment and gives $D_\Gamma(n)=0$, so both questions
have answer ``no''.
For $k=2$, the first two examples are $(x,y,z)$ with
$D(n)=n^2(n-1)$ and $(x,y,x)$ with $D(n)=n(n-1)$.

sections.title: Terms, interpretations, and the output image

blocks.raw:
\label{sec:language}
Fix a finite nonempty set $X$ of variables, also called \emph{source
variables}, and a finite signature $\Sigma$: a set of function symbols
with a specified nonnegative integer arity for each symbol. Terms are
finite rooted expressions over $X$ and $\Sigma$, with ordered arguments.
A symbol of arity zero is a constant symbol. Syntactic equality means
literal equality of expressions using the same symbol and variable
names; no algebraic identities or cancellation rules are imposed.
An interpretation $I$ on a nonempty set $A$ assigns one function
$I_f:A^{\operatorname{arity}(f)}\to A$ to each $f\in\Sigma$.
Every such function is defined on its entire domain, with no prescribed
values. For an assignment $a:X\to A$, the value $u^I(a)$ of a term is
defined recursively. All occurrences of $f$ use the same $I_f$.

An instance $\Gamma$ consists of variables $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$,
a finite signature $\Sigma$, an output tuple
$\mathbf t=(t_1,\ldots,t_r)$, and a finite list $\Delta$ of tests
$u\ne v$ between terms over $X$ and $\Sigma$.
For an interpretation $I$ on a finite nonempty set $A$, define
\[
 C_I=\{a\in A^m:u^I(a)\ne v^I(a)
                    \text{ for every }(u\ne v)\in\Delta\}.
\]
The output map is
$\mathbf t^I(a)=(t_1^I(a),\ldots,t_r^I(a))$.
Its image on the allowed inputs is $\mathbf t^I(C_I)\subseteq A^r$.
For $n\ge1$, the dispersion is
\[
 D_\Gamma(n)=\DD_n(\mathbf t,\Delta)
       =\max_{I\text{ on }[n]}|\mathbf t^I(C_I)|.
\]

For the complexity statements, names, arities, variables, output and
test lists, and ordered argument lists are explicitly encoded in binary.

sections.title: Reduction from a fixed finitely presented group

blocks.raw:
A finite quotient of a group $G$ means a finite group $Q$ together with
a surjective homomorphism $G\to Q$. A word is \emph{separated} in such
a quotient if its image is not the identity. Bridson and Wilton
\cite[Theorem 2.1]{BW}, deriving a consequence of Slobodskoi's construction
\cite{Slo}, prove that there is a fixed finitely presented group $G$
for which the set
\[
 \{w:\text{$w$ has nonidentity image in some finite quotient of $G$}\}
\]
is recursively enumerable and undecidable. Thus an algorithm can
eventually find a separating finite quotient whenever one exists,
but no algorithm decides for every input word whether one exists.
The presentation is fixed; the input consists only of the word.
We first describe our reduction for an arbitrary finite presentation.

For every finite presentation $G$ and signed word $w$,

There is a fixed finite presentation $G$ such that, given a signed
word $w$, deciding whether $D_{G,w}(n)=n(n-1)$ for some $n\ge2$ is

signature, a fixed number of tests, and just two variables and two
outputs. Their positive instances are recursively enumerable but not
decidable, and their complement is not recursively enumerable.

Bridson--Wilton state their theorem for freely reduced words, meaning
words with no adjacent inverse pair $a_i a_i^{-1}$ or $a_i^{-1}a_i$.
Such a word is already a valid signed input word here. Conversely,
removing adjacent inverse pairs is computable and preserves evaluation
in every group, hence preserves separation in finite quotients.
The reduction theorem therefore gives the same exact decision problem
for arbitrary signed words.
This does \emph{not} license cancellation in the terms under arbitrary
interpretations: $p_i$ and $m_i$ need not be inverse functions.
Cancellation preserves their evaluation only after the required inverse
laws hold, as they do when the pair bound is attained.

sections.title: Scope and the problem without tests

blocks.raw:
\label{sec:open}
The decision problems use one finite set for all variables and function values.
For each fixed $k\ge2$, undecidability already holds with $k$ variables,
all retained as outputs, a fixed finite unary signature and a fixed
number of tests. Only the nested expression for the input word varies.
The tests compare computed expressions as well as variables.
Writing a computed term as a new variable with a defining equation does
not make it an independent source variable: its value is determined
by the original inputs. The reduction therefore proves no
undecidability result for the narrower language in which tests may
compare only source variables.

Without disequality tests, finite square term bijectivity asks the
following: given $k$ terms in $k$ variables, does some interpretation
on a finite set $A$, with $|A|\ge2$, make the resulting map
$A^k\to A^k$ bijective? This problem remains open in general.
Paper~2 \cite{Paper2} identifies an image of size $|A|^k$ for such a
map with bijectivity, and gives padding reductions from the case $k=3$
to the problem of attaining the full output set at every fixed output
dimension at least three. Those reductions do not prove undecidability
and are not used here. An unconditional polynomial-time/undecidable
separation for dispersion without disequality tests remains open.
The present bounds also concern a different quantity from the number
of solutions of an arbitrary equation system or the entropy and
guessing number of a graph; they do not imply that those quantities
are integer-valued or efficiently computable.

abstractHtml: Term coding provides a common algebraic framework for network coding, index coding and problems in extremal combinatorics. We exhibit a decision problem in which lowering an output threshold by just one changes the complexity from polynomial time to undecidability: no algorithm then halts with the correct answer on every input. The problem concerns dispersion, the maximum number of distinct output tuples obtainable by interpreting the function symbols in a tuple of terms on a finite alphabet. We restrict inputs by inequalities between terms and ask whether a given instance meets a prescribed output threshold for some alphabet size at least two. Both thresholds are considered on the same class of instances. A machine-checked Lean development and an interactive presentation of the paper accompany this work (GitHub: https://github.com/SR123/term-coding-disequality-lean; DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22727895); Section 8 specifies its external input and verification limits.

s2-1.title: Terms and their meanings
s2-1.body: There are two different objects to keep separate: a term is a finite expression; an interpretation tells us how to evaluate it. The functions are shared across every occurrence of a symbol.

s2-6.title: What input length measures
s2-6.body: The complexity variable is the actual number of supplied bits. On a DAG, process children first and identify each node by its symbol and ordered list of already canonical child names. This avoids unfolding repeated subterms into an exponentially larger tree.

headline-bound.body: A computable upper bound would turn the unbounded search for an alphabet into a finite search. At each size, all interpretations and assignments form finite sets. Searching them would decide the non-strict problem, contradicting the reduction. No efficiency assumption is needed for that contradiction.

s1-7.title: Value, bit length and output tables
s1-7.body: For fixed k, s^(k+1) is a polynomial in s. For variable k the value may be large, but positivity implies k+1≤ρ≤s. The binary length of s^(k+1) is bounded by (k+1) times the binary length of s. This bounds the integer describing the alphabet, not tables on that alphabet.

s1-8.title: Saturation turns tests into laws
s1-8.body: If every distinct pair is admitted, fixing a and choosing b=F(a) rules out F(a)≠a. Applying this separately to each law term forces all inverse and relator identities. Padding then preserves exactly whether saturation is possible.

s1-9.title: Routing and the sharper upper bound
s1-9.body: The labels are part of alphabet elements. They tell a shared operation which subterm it is evaluating and simultaneously separate syntactically distinct sides of tests. s1-10.title: Approximation does not decide saturation
s1-10.body: A shift interpretation makes every nonempty input word move every point when n exceeds its written length. Each law can then exclude at most one extra second coordinate in each row. Losing at most Mn pairs gives density approaching one, even if losing zero pairs is impossible.

s1-11.title: Three exact examples
s1-11.body: Distinct retained variables make all allowed assignments distinct outputs. Repeating the last coordinate loses that free coordinate without changing the number of output positions. The final test x₁≠x₁ is deliberately impossible: it removes every assignment and makes the dispersion zero, so both questions have answer “no”. These constructions show that the decision problems are nonvacuous.

s1-12.title: An easy subset of a hard language
s1-12.body: A strict positive instance is non-strict positive because bₖ(n)+1≥bₖ(n). Inclusion alone imposes no relation in the reverse direction between the complexities of recognising the sets. The arithmetic separation bₖ(n)+1<bₖ₊₁(n) gives the alternating sequence.

external-group.title: The external finite-group theorem
external-group.body: The imported mathematical input says that some fixed finite presentation has a noncomputable finite-quotient separation predicate. This project proves implications from that hypothesis; it does not prove the Slobodskoi–Bridson–Wilton theorem. In Lean, the hypothesis appears explicitly as ¬ ComputablePred (HasFiniteQuotient rels), rather than as a new hidden axiom. The paper cites Bridson–Wilton, Theorem 2.1.

s5-2.title: The compiler keeps the written order of letters
s5-2.body: A signed letter chooses one of two independent unary symbols. A list of letters becomes nested application, with the last letter applied first. Two inverse laws per generator and one law per relator are retained as a list, including repetitions and empty relators.

word-order.title: Why the permutation product matches nesting
word-order.body: Group words multiply from left to right as written; acting on a point applies the rightmost permutation first. The evaluation bridge proves that nested unary evaluation equals the action of that product. Inverse cancellation is only available after the tables satisfy the inverse laws.

s5-3.title: The actual encoded tests
s5-3.body: The compiler emits the guard x≠y, a disequality L(x)≠y for every law, and the word test τw(x)≠x. The output pair itself is unchanged. The semantic bridge proves that the allowed image of these terms is exactly the pair set used in the counting argument.

s5-4.title: The equivalence has two constructive directions

s5-5.title: From saturation to a separating quotient
s5-5.body: First extract the everywhere-valid laws. Two-sided inverses turn pᵢ into permutations. Relators equal to the identity allow the universal property of the presented group to produce a homomorphism into the finite permutation group. The word moves every point, so its permutation is not the identity. Taking the image subgroup makes the homomorphism surjective.

presentation-property.body: The group is constructed as a quotient of a free group by the normal closure of the relators. s5-6.title: From a finite quotient to saturation
s5-6.body: Left multiplication by a nonidentity group element has no fixed point: qb=b implies q=1 by cancellation. The regular action satisfies all presentation laws. Thus all distinct pairs satisfy all tests. A group with a nonidentity element has at least two elements.

compiler-size.title: Why the written compiler is small
compiler-size.body: Each letter contributes one unary application node. The inverse-law prefix has fixed length for a fixed presentation, and the relators are copied once. The exact node-length formulas expose this linear size calculation. The executable compiler is also proved computable; the source-level linear construction argument explains the paper’s polynomial bound.

s5-8.body: At each alphabet size there are finitely many tables and assignments, so the fixed-size threshold can be computed. Searching sizes finds every positive case. If the complement were enumerable too, dovetailing the two searches would decide the language.

s5-9.title: Free reduction belongs to group evaluation
s5-9.body: The reduction algorithm removes adjacent opposite signed letters. It preserves the value of a word in every group, and hence finite-quotient separation. It does not preserve evaluation under arbitrary unrelated unary functions. The latter distinction is essential for the shift construction.

s5-10.title: Empty words and the limit of the complexity claim
s5-10.body: The empty word evaluates to x by definition, so its last test is impossible. Removing that one decidable negative case cannot make an undecidable language decidable: a purported decision procedure for the remainder could handle the empty case separately. Enumerability plus undecidability does not establish completeness.

padding-step.title: Why padding gives an exact product
padding-step.body: The new variables occur in no old output or test. For each old allowed output, all n^(k−2) choices of new coordinates occur, independently. Conversely, projecting any new output onto its first two coordinates gives an old allowed output. This proves equality of sets, then cardinalities. The multiplier is independent of the interpretation, so it commutes with taking the maximum.

s6-1.body: The exact product identity multiplies the pair bound by n^(k−2). This factor is positive for n≥2, so reaching the new upper bound is equivalent to reaching the old one. All k variables are outputs, forcing cut size k.

strict-arithmetic.title: Both sides of the strict criterion
strict-arithmetic.body: If the cut is at most k, monotonicity of bρ in ρ and the sharp cut bound prevent any strict witness. If the cut is at least k+1, routing at n=s^(k+1) gives at least n^k outputs. Since n^(k−1)≥1, this reaches bₖ(n)+1. An identical-side test is a separate immediate rejection case.

s6-3.body: Compute the encoded length, compute its alleged bound, and run the finite-size decision at every size up to that bound. If a witness exists, the bound promises one in this finite range. If none is found, the instance is negative. This contradicts the externally conditional noncomputability theorem.

machine-model.title: What one machine step means
machine-model.body: A configuration consists of a program counter and a memory function with natural-number cells. Primitive instructions copy constants or cells, load and store indirectly, add, subtract with truncation, and jump or halt. The step relation states one transition. Run composes finitely many such transitions and adds their costs.

machine-compilation.title: Why the structured program is the same RAM computation
machine-compilation.body: The intermediate command language offers sequencing, branches and loops. Compilation replaces these constructs by primitive instructions and numerical jump destinations. The compiler correctness theorem preserves the final memory and the exact number of machine steps.

machine-cost.title: Why unit steps also give a polynomial bit cost
machine-cost.body: The allowed arithmetic can increase the maximum stored bit length by at most one per step, after accounting for constants. Instruction cost charges the bit lengths of accessed values and indirect addresses. A run of n steps therefore has cost bounded using its initial bit bound plus n. Composing this with the polynomial step bound yields a polynomial cost bound.

s6-7.body: If the third term uses only x and y, the pair determines it, giving a two-term cut. A path from another variable to that term cannot pass through the variable vertices x or y. It supplies the third disjoint path. Routing then gives the cubic lower bound and its explicit comparison with n^(5/2).

s6-8.body: When x and y are not outputs, satisfying x≠y places no restriction on the independent output values z,w. At n≥2, choose a distinct x,y pair and then any z,w. This gives all n² outputs although the output cut is two.

shift-step.body: Both positive and formal inverse symbols are assigned z↦z+1 modulo n. A written word of length L therefore evaluates as z↦z+L. If 0<L<n, its residue is nonzero, so no point is fixed. Nothing here asserts that the formal inverse symbols actually give inverses.

s7-1.body: The shift construction gives a fixed-point-free word. Row counting loses at most M additional second coordinates per first coordinate. s7-2.title: Count the excluded second coordinates
s7-2.body: At a fixed a, the guard forbids a and each of the M laws can forbid at most one further value. These values may coincide, which only improves the lower bound. Since the word has no fixed point, no entire row is removed. Multiply the row lower bound by n.

There is therefore no decision procedure for saturation hidden in the computable approximation.

s8-1.title: Computed nodes are not additional independent sources
s8-1.body: Flattening introduces names for determined values. Its unique-extension theorem does not turn those values into arbitrary source inputs. The undecidability reduction therefore remains a result about tests on computed terms, and does not settle the narrower source-only test language.

s8-4.title: The precise machine theorem and its remaining boundary
s8-4.body: The fixed RAM program is proved to halt with the answer decideBits for every input. The accepted language is StrictBits. The time polynomial is uniform in the encoded instance and the binary degree. A simulation of this logarithmic-cost RAM by a multitape Turing machine is not formalised in the project.

s8-5.title: How to audit the correspondence
s8-5.body: Start from a paper paragraph, expand the mathematical reasoning, then open its exact Lean statements. Check the quantifiers and hypotheses before following the proof. Source steps expose recorded before/after goals. The kernel view exposes the proof expression, implicit arguments, dependencies and logical primitives. These exports aid inspection; the Lean kernel, not the web interface or its English explanations, checks the proof.

verification-correspondence.title: Two different things to inspect
verification-correspondence.body: A successfully checked proof establishes its formal type. It does not establish that an English paragraph was translated faithfully. The correspondence notes explain identifications such as finite supremum versus maximum, pointwise identity versus equality of functions, and encoded validity versus membership of the input class. They are authored commentary and remain open to mathematical review.

abstract.title: The paper’s main message
abstract.body: The two languages have the same input class and differ only by one unit in the output threshold. The strict side has a uniform polynomial machine algorithm. The non-strict side inherits undecidability from the stated external group theorem. The formal links below separate the semantic, algorithmic and external obligations.
